The line "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be" refuses panic. It does not deny that the day is real. It denies that the day gets the last word. Treasure is the better word, and it can sit with you while you answer the message you have been avoiding. Choose one person and wish them treasure without announcing it. A text, a glass of water, a patient answer. Matthew 6:21 becomes yours when it moves toward someone else. End by telling the truth: you needed treasure today, and Matthew 6:21 did not shame you for needing it. Gratitude is the right last step. Then close the panel and go be a person in a real room. Stay with treasure long enough for it to become a tone of voice, not only an idea. Matthew 6:21 can survive contact with a real afternoon.

text: The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.
devotional: Life is not a mood you manufacture. John 10:10 treats it as a gift you can receive while the coffee cools and the list stays long. The public words are old and plain: "The thief cometh not, but for to steal." They do not decorate the day. They tell the truth about where life comes from. You are not asked to feel impressive. You are asked to stay near the God who spoke this line and still keeps company with tired people. If someone in the house is short with you, answer one sentence more gently than you feel. That is life with shoes on. John 10:10 was never only for private thoughts. It is for the way a voice sounds in a kitchen. When midnight comes in Phoenix, the verse will change. Until then, John 10:10 is your companion and life is your practice. One day. One word. That is a faithful way to live until you sleep.

text: I sought the LORD , and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears.
devotional: Read Psalm 34:4 slowly enough to hear the word freedom without rushing past it. A verse is wasted when it is only a slogan. It helps when it becomes a way of walking. Notice how little Psalm 34:4 wastes. "I sought the LORD , and he heard me." A whole practice of freedom can hide inside a sentence that short. You do not need a new personality today. You need a true sentence you are willing to trust for the next hour. Try one small practice. When you feel the pull to hurry, pause and name freedom out loud. Then finish the task in front of you without adding a speech about how behind you are. The verse is meant to lighten the grip, not to add another item to the list. God's care is not smaller than this screen, and it is not too large for it either. Psalm 34:4 fits in a kitchen. Freedom fits in a person. Take both into whatever is left of the day, and do not carry more than that.

text: There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit.
devotional: There is room in an ordinary afternoon for mercy. Romans 8:1 was written for people with errands, not only for people with spare time. Say "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are" without trying to sound holy. Romans 8:1 is sturdy enough for a normal voice. Mercy becomes practical when it changes the tone of one reply, one chore, one apology. Before you open a screen again, sit with the verse long enough to notice your shoulders. Drop them. Mercy is allowed to be physical. God is not offended by a body that needs a slower breath. You do not have to keep this whole devotional. Keep the reference and the word Mercy. If those two stay with you while you wash a cup or answer a child, the verse has done its work. Stay with mercy long enough for it to become a tone of voice, not only an idea. Romans 8:1 can survive contact with a real afternoon.

text: For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD .
devotional: Before the kitchen gets noisy, Isaiah 55:8 is enough for one honest minute. The word for today is Trust. You do not have to solve the whole day. You only have to let one true sentence land. Hold the short phrase "For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your." It is small enough to remember while you drive, cook, or wait. Trust grows in those in-between minutes more than it grows in speeches. Let the phrase interrupt a spiral. Say it once, then do the next simple thing. Write Trust on a scrap of paper and leave it where you will see it after lunch. When you see it, ask a simpler question than "how do I fix everything?" Ask "what would trust look like in the next ten minutes?" Then do that. Let the last word of the afternoon be trust, not the loudest worry. Isaiah 55:8 has already said something better. Receive it again, simply, and let the board go quiet.

text: Depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it.
devotional: Psalm 34:14 does not shout. It sits beside the ordinary work of peace and waits until you are willing to hear it. Glance is a small screen for a large mercy, and this verse is sized for that screen. If the verse feels larger than your morning, start with the fragment you can carry: "Depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue." Peace often arrives as a smaller mercy than we requested. Receive the size you are given. That is enough to keep you kind. When the afternoon slumps, do not bargain with shame. Return to the sentence you already read. Peace can begin again at 3 o'clock. The day is not ruined because the morning was messy. The point of today's verse is not that you become impressive. The point is that peace is near, and near is enough. Psalm 34:14 can go with you into an unremarkable evening. That is a good place for faith to live.

text: A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.
devotional: Some mornings ask for a plan. This one asks for joy. Proverbs 17:22 gives you a place to stand while the calendar fills up around you. "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but." Read it as a promise you can lean on, not a test you must pass. Joy is offered before you have earned the afternoon. That order matters. Receive first, then work. Take a two-minute walk, even if it is only to the end of the driveway. Repeat the reference once. Let joy be the pace of your steps. Coming back, do the next right thing and leave the rest unargued. Leave joy where you can find it: in the way you lock the door, in the way you say goodnight, in the way you stop rehearsing the argument. Proverbs 17:22 will still be true when the house is dark. You can rest without finishing every thought.

text: Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
devotional: The day will offer plenty of noise. Ecclesiastes 4:9 offers a quieter center, and its theme is Friendship. Carry that one word into the next conversation instead of carrying every worry at once. "Two are better than one; because they have a good." Those words have outlived the week they were first heard. They can outlive this one too. Friendship here is not a performance. It is a steadying hand on the shoulder, the kind that does not need an audience. At the next meal, let Ecclesiastes 4:9 be the quiet blessing. You do not need to preach it. Thank God for friendship in one sentence, then pass the food. Holiness can be that ordinary and still be real. Tonight, do not grade the day. Remember Ecclesiastes 4:9 and the single word Friendship. If you were kinder than you expected, give thanks. If you were not, mercy is still on duty. Tomorrow's verse will come at midnight, Phoenix time. This one only has to carry you until then.
